content: The following information provides a detailed overview of the dosing, indications, interactions, contraindications, and safety considerations for black cohosh (Actaea racemosa), also known as baneberry or black snakeroot, when used alone or in combination with other substances: Dosing Information: Liquid Extract (1:1, 90% alcohol tincture): Administer 3–2 mL orally per day. Liquid Extract (1:10, 60% alcohol tincture): Administer 2–4 mL orally per day. Tablet Formulation: Administer 20–80 mg orally twice daily. Tablets are standardized to contain 1 mg of triterpene glycosides per 20 mg tablet. Indications: Black cohosh is used for the following conditions: Cough and sore throat Dysmenorrhea (painful menstruation) Dyspepsia (indigestion) Labor induction Menopausal symptoms Nervous tension Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) Rheumatism Effectiveness: Likely Effective: For managing vasomotor symptoms associated with menopause (e.g., hot flashes). Possibly Effective: For premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and dysmenorrhea. Drug Interactions: 1. Iobenguane I-131: Black cohosh may reduce the efficacy of iobenguane by interfering with catecholamine uptake into cells. It is recommended to discontinue interfering drugs for at least five half-lives before administering iobenguane and to avoid reintroducing these drugs until at least seven days after the iobenguane dose. 2. Nevirapine: Co-administration with black cohosh may increase the risk of hepatotoxicity due to pharmacodynamic synergism. The significance of this interaction is unknown. 3. Tamoxifen: Black cohosh may enhance the effects of tamoxifen through pharmacodynamic synergism. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. 4. Tenofovir DF: Co-administration may increase the risk of hepatotoxicity due to pharmacodynamic synergism. The significance of this interaction is unknown. 5. Zidovudine: Black cohosh may increase the toxicity of zidovudine through pharmacodynamic synergism, with an associated risk of hepatotoxicity. The clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. Adverse Effects: Common side effects include: Cramping Dizziness Gastrointestinal upset Headache Sweating Weight gain Rash Overdose Symptoms: Bradycardia (slow heart rate) Central nervous system disturbances Nausea and vomiting Visual disturbances Contraindications: Black cohosh should not be used in individuals with the following conditions: Breast cancer Endometrial cancer Endometriosis Hormone-sensitive conditions Ovarian cancer Pregnancy Lactation Uterine fibroids Safety Concerns: Black cohosh may be associated with liver damage. Pregnancy Category: Unsafe for use during pregnancy. Lactation: Unsafe for use during breastfeeding. Summary of Pregnancy and Lactation Categories: Category A: Generally acceptable. Controlled studies in pregnant women show no evidence of fetal risk. However, black cohosh does not fall under this category and is considered unsafe during pregnancy and lactation. This information highlights the importance of careful consideration when using black cohosh, particularly in individuals with pre-existing conditions or those taking other medications.
